_comment: The DECIDED numbers behind the R-register gates. Skills and the recipe router READ this file — a gate with no number here is prose, not a gate. Tracked in git; change via PR, not ad-hoc edits. Every prose field beside a number is the rule the number enforces and the honesty clause that goes with it; a document may restate the rule but never promise more than the clause allows.

r5_budget.metering_source: the RUNNER supplies the figure: an orchestrator's own per-run API usage accounting when one exists (authoritative), or the Claude Code session's `total_cost_usd` when run headless or interactively. The loop passes --budget-spent to recipe_router.py at every stage gate. UNITS, because the name says usd and that can mislead: `total_cost_usd` is the harness's own CLIENT-SIDE ESTIMATE, computed from token counts at public list prices — Claude Code's headless docs say both of its figures 'are client-side estimates and can differ from your actual bill'. There are two billing postures, and stack.config `runner.billing_posture` records which one a deployment is in. Under `subscription` (the CLI authenticates with a Claude.ai subscription and no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN is set) NOTHING IS BILLED for a run, so this cap bounds a list-price-EQUIVALENT consumption number, not money. Under `api` (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set — those take precedence over a subscription credential) the run bills as metered API usage and this cap bounds real dollars; see pr_review_loop.per_day_usd_cap_rule's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY paragraph and pr_review.sh's exit 28 guard. The one line item this cap never sees is the embedding provider behind qa-kb (kb.config `embedding.provider`), which is metered by that provider whatever the runner's posture is.
r5_budget.enforcement: recipe_router.py compares spend >= cap and returns stop-budget. When --budget-cap is not passed, the router reads per_loop_usd_cap from THIS file (0 no longer means 'no cap' by silent default). HONESTY, and it has two halves — do not quote one without the other. (1) MECHANISM: until a runner actually supplies --budget-spent, the breaker is a declared cap with a tested comparator, NOT an enforced gate — documents must not call it 'hard' beyond this. The one place it IS enforced today is pr_review.sh, which hands this number to `claude --max-budget-usd` so the harness ends the session itself. (2) UNITS: under the subscription posture the number is not dollars charged — see metering_source. A document may call this a consumption cap, a runaway backstop, or a proxy for rate-limit-window burn; it may NOT call it a budget, a bill, or spend-in-dollars unless the api posture is actually in force.
r5_budget.note_sandbox_cap: the sandbox adapter's concurrent-sandbox cap (adapters.sandbox.config.max_concurrent) is a RESOURCE bound (sandbox count), not the R5 spend breaker — do not count it as R5 coverage.

mechanisms: per-loop sandbox isolation: the sandbox adapter provisions a unique branch, port offset and (when the stack supplies a clone command) database per loop, and its registry is mutated only under an exclusive fcntl lock (tested under a parallel race)
shared-brain writes: kb.py optimistic concurrency — pass --expect-version on every app_map UPDATE (version_conflict on a lost race, harness-tested)

scheduled agents: one shared cross-agent lock (.claude/loops/lib/agent_lock.sh) that every scheduled runner takes before real work, so two timers never overlap in a model call or a brain write; the loser skips (exit 0) because every queue is durable
r4_concurrency.honesty: there is NO general file/resource lock primitive and none is claimed. A writer that omits --expect-version last-write-wins; every app_map UPDATE MUST pass it.

r7_flake_quarantine.rule: quarantine a test (kb quarantine flakiness --on) when flake_rate >= 0.3 over >= 5 recorded runs; below min_runs, keep recording data points without quarantining. Surface every quarantine in the regression report — never silently drop a test.
r7_flake_quarantine.suite_health_ship_gate: not yet wired: suite flake rate does not feed ship_preflight (tracked as future R7 work, not claimed).

staging_only.representation: kb_control flag 'staging_only' in the brain (seeded true; read via `kb flag --name staging_only --status`). ship_preflight.sh reads it FAIL CLOSED (unreadable = true) and it sets ONLY prod_deploy_allowed (false while true), which the preflight's prod-lane guard enforces (exit 7 on a push to any branch matching stack.config `deploy.prod_lane_branch_patterns`; an empty list means no push is a deploy). It does NOT set dry_run: dry_run comes only from SHIP_DRY_RUN=1, and PRs open live otherwise — a PR is the human review gate, not a deploy. Flipping to prod posture is a deliberate `kb flag --name staging_only --off --by <human>` — never a script edit.

defect_pr_threads.rule: The most comment threads a defect/feature loop may post on ITS OWN PR, across every ship of it (infra-ship Step 6). The expected count is ZERO: a thread is posted only for an item that passes the must-read test in infra-ship/references/pr-thread-bar.md (the reviewer must act before merge, getting it wrong costs something real, and the consequence lands outside the changed lines). The SELECTION is enforced by infra-ship/scripts/select_pr_threads.py (tested): it takes only must_read:true entries with a recognised must_read_reason and an ask, counts every loop thread already on the PR (--existing) against this cap, never posts one twice, and renders anything past the cap as a Before merging section at the top of the description — moved, never dropped. What actually LANDED is checked by infra-ship/scripts/audit_pr_threads.py (before/after read-back of the PR through the vcs_host adapter: a thread from the runner that the funnel did not post is noise_thread, more loop threads than this is over_cap_on_pr; both exit 3 into ship.json thread_audit and the pr_threads_* metrics) — the POST itself is the agent's, so the audit is detection, not prevention. 0 means no threads at all. --max can only LOWER this; a missing or invalid value falls back to 2 and says so in cap_source. Calibration, stated as the lesson rather than the incident: under a flag-every-decision rule a two-bug PR collected over a dozen threads and the reviewer called every one noise; under this bar the same PR gets 0. NOT the same as pr_review_loop.max_threads_per_pr, which caps the findings the PR-review loop posts on the PRs it reviews — by default (author_scope own) the runner's own PRs, which INCLUDES published defect-loop PRs. To keep the two lanes apart, infra-ship labels every loop PR with the loop label (stack.config `integrations.pr_review.loop_pr_label`, default agent-loop) and dev-pr-feed's unreviewed queue skips it (LOOP_PR_INCLUDE_LOOP_PRS=1 overrides), so a loop PR carries only this lane's threads.

pr_review_loop.rule: dev-loop-pr-review reviews at most this many PRs per tick. 2 is MEASURED, not argued: budget roughly 900s of model call per pull request (one real PR is a large diff, a six-specialist review and a report), plus this runner's own pre- and post-session work (queue read, posting-guard build, hygiene sweep, kb receipt) which sits OUTSIDE the session timeout. Two of those fit the scheduler job's 2400s --timeout with roughly 600s of headroom, and the whole tick still finishes inside pr_feed's 2700s tick-lock TTL — the harder of the two ceilings, because a tick that outlives its own lock lets the NEXT tick see 'stale' and start sweeping while this one is still posting. Three do not fit: 3 x 900 = 2700s is the entire timeout with nothing left for the report. Capacity is not the binding constraint — hourly x 2 is 48 PRs/day against a board that produces a handful, and the queue is durable and keyed on PR id + head commit, so an unreviewed third PR is simply still unreviewed an hour later. THIS NUMBER AND THE JOB'S --timeout ARE ONE DECISION: change either and re-derive the other from the per-PR figure. It lives HERE and deliberately NOT in the job's arguments — pr_review.sh reads it from this file, a --limit in the job definition OVERRIDES it (the job sidecar's preflight then prints 'ProgramArguments OVERRIDE loop-limits.json' and this tracked decision stops being the effective one), and two copies of one number are how two numbers come to disagree. Raise it on measured duration_s from pr-review.log, never on the arithmetic above.
pr_review_loop.author_scope_rule: own | all | others. The template ships 'own': the tick reviews only the pull requests whose author is the identity the vcs_host adapter resolves for the runner. WHAT WIDENING MEANS, concretely: 'all' reviews every active non-draft PR targeting the configured base branch, COLLEAGUES' INCLUDED, and with --live armed its comment threads carry the RUNNER'S OWN vcs_host identity — on someone else's pull request they appear to come from that person, not from a bot. That is the whole reason this key exists and the whole reason the default is 'own'. THIS FILE ALONE CANNOT WIDEN IT, by design: pr_review.sh REFUSES a --live tick whose scope is not 'own' unless --scope is also on the command line (exit 25, event=refused reason=live_wide_scope_not_reaffirmed), so a widened value here must be matched by a --scope/<value> pair in the scheduler job's arguments or the job refuses every hour and reviews nothing. LOOP_PR_AUTHOR_SCOPE in the environment is IGNORED by the runner and says so on stderr. TO WIDEN, both halves and in this order: set this key, add the --scope pair to the job definition, then install.sh --label com.loops.pr-review --check (the scope and posture lines flip) and re-install. TO REVERT, the same two edits in reverse. Changing one half only is safe in one direction and useless in the other — file 'own' + job --scope all still comments on everyone (the flag wins), while file 'all' + no flag refuses the tick. Re-decide max_threads_per_pr in the same edit (see that rule).
pr_review_loop.posting_note: The template ships dry-run: a tick does the full review and writes a byte-faithful preview of the payload plus the tick report, and nothing reaches the vcs host. READ THIS KEY AS A RECORD, NOT A GATE: nothing reads posting_default at run time. The actual switch is --live in the scheduler job's arguments — pr_review.sh defaults to dry-run, and the generated posting guard STRIPS --live from every pr_feed call on a dry-run tick, so a session cannot type its way live. This key exists so the tracked decision and the armed job can be compared: the job sidecar prints both in preflight and warns when they disagree. Independent of it, dev-pr-feed FAILS CLOSED on the R9 pause flag before any live post, and a --live tick refuses to start at all with no seen-ledger unless --first-run says a blank one is intended. TO GO LIVE: add --live to the job definition (that is the half that actually posts), set this to 'live' so the record matches, then --check and re-install — after the hand-run gate in scheduler/FIRST-RUN-pr-review.md. TO REVERT: remove --live, set this back to 'dry-run', --check, re-install.
pr_review_loop.max_threads_per_pr_rule: The most comment threads ONE `post` call may land on ONE pull request — previews included, because a dry-run preview is byte-for-byte what the live tick would send. ENFORCED, mechanically: pr_review.sh generates a posting guard (build_posting_guard) that ranks the postable findings critical > high > medium > low, stamps everything past this cap withheld:true + a withheld_reason naming the cap, writes findings-capped-<pr>.json, substitutes THAT file into --findings, and echoes runner_volume_cap back on the result. Criticals are dropped last, and the surplus still rides in review.json and the tick report — the cap trades comment volume for report-only visibility, never the top of the list. HONESTY, four ways: (1) it bounds a POST CALL, not a PR's lifetime — a PR re-enters the queue at every new head commit, so exposure on one PR is this number x pushes reviewed; (2) a withheld finding is NOT re-offered, because the same tick marks the PR reviewed at that head commit — it comes back only if the author pushes again; (3) it is not a sandbox: if the guard cannot build (mktemp) the session is handed pr_feed.py directly and NO cap applies, which is why the runner prints which pr_feed the session got ('posting guard armed …') and names the source of this number beside it; (4) read_limits validates only > 0 — 0 or a negative means FALL BACK to pr_review.sh's MAX_THREADS_FALLBACK literal (3, so the fallback cannot silently loosen this), never 'off', and unlike prs_per_tick (LIMIT_CEILING=10) nothing ceilings this key, so a fat-fingered 50 is accepted in silence and attributed to this file. WHY 3: it is the number that is right for a scope wider than 'own', and the template keeps it even at 'own' so widening the scope later does not also require remembering to tighten this. The reviewer-perspective argument: several bot threads on your own pull request is a thorough review; the same number on a colleague's is a pile-on, and the first impression this loop makes on a colleague decides whether it is welcome at all. The cost of 3 is VISIBLE — guard_interventions= on every event=end line, and the report names every withheld finding with its reason — so a cap that bites too often shows up as data rather than as silence, which is why the loose direction is not the safe default. Revisit on measured guard_interventions after a couple of weeks of ticks: if it fires on anything but big PRs, the review BAR is what drifted, not this cap.
pr_review_loop.per_day_usd_cap_rule: The aggregate ceiling on THIS loop's own recorded CONSUMPTION in one UTC day. WHAT THE NUMBER IS, first, because everything below depends on it: it is `total_cost_usd` read out of `claude --output-format json` — the harness's OWN CLIENT-SIDE ESTIMATE, computed from token counts at public list prices. Claude Code's headless docs say it in as many words: both figures 'are client-side estimates and can differ from your actual bill'. Under the subscription posture (stack.config `runner.billing_posture`: the CLI authenticates with a Claude.ai subscription and no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set in the shell or in the job definition) NOTHING IS BILLED for a tick and this figure is a list-price EQUIVALENT, not money charged. Read every USD-looking number in this key as list-price-equivalent consumption unless the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY paragraph below applies — a gate that promises more than the code delivers is exactly what this repo forbids. WHAT IT IS FOR, then, since under that posture it is not a budget: a runaway-consumption backstop — a wedged or looping job that starts 24 sessions a day is caught by a number rather than by someone eventually noticing — and a usable PROXY for how much of the rolling rate-limit window this job is burning. Those two jobs do not need the number to be money, which is why the gate is kept and kept enforced. THE REAL CONSTRAINT under subscription auth, which nothing here measures: the rolling rate-limit window, SHARED with all Claude.ai and Claude Code usage on the account. That is the resource that actually runs out; an unattended hourly tick competes for it with the human at the keyboard. There is no silent fallback from subscription to metered API — exhaustion is a hard HTTP 429 and the session stops (pr_review.sh exit 29, outcome=anthropic-rate-limited: not a fault, not counted toward the consecutive-stuck counter, comes back next hour). No window meter exists anywhere in this system. The consumption figure below correlates with window burn; it does not measure it, and must not be quoted as if it did. THE ONE LINE ITEM THIS CAP NEVER SEES: the embedding provider behind qa-kb (kb.config `embedding.provider` — every expectations / fix_lessons write and every semantic search embeds). That is a real API key against that provider's own balance or quota, it can hit its own 429, and it never appears in total_cost_usd at all; nothing in this file caps it. HOW THE GATE WORKS — all of this is mechanically true in either posture. The per-TICK ceiling is r5_budget.per_loop_usd_cap, which pr_review.sh passes to the harness as `claude --max-budget-usd` (that half IS harness-enforced — the session simply ends). This key exists because a per-session cap is not the exposure: an hourly job ticks 24x/day, and 24 x the per-tick ceiling is a day's consumption that nothing in the chain summed. The model call runs with --output-format json, the runner reads the harness's own total_cost_usd out of it, accumulates it per UTC day in pr-review-runner-state.json (record_spend), and exits 26 without starting another model call once the day's total >= this number. WHAT IT DOES NOT BOUND, plainly: (1) it is an ADMISSION gate checked once, before the call — a tick admitted at 59.99 still runs to its own 15.0 ceiling, so the true daily bound is per_day_usd_cap + per_loop_usd_cap = 75 at these numbers, and no runbook, report or PR description may print 60 as the maximum; (2) a tick whose session reports no total_cost_usd (watchdog TERM/KILL at --timeout, a crash, non-JSON stdout) cannot be measured, so it is CHARGED THE PER-TICK CEILING (r5_budget.per_loop_usd_cap) instead of 0 and counted separately as spend_assumed_usd / spend_unmeasured_ticks in the state file. That number is deliberately pessimistic — the tick may have consumed far less — and it is labelled `assumed` on stderr and in the log (event=spend_assumed). Reading it as 0 was worse, and was the hole this key exists to close: a wedged session TERMed every hour is 24 ticks, each free to run to its own ceiling, i.e. the entire 24 x 15 exposure back while the counter reads 0.0000 and every tick is admitted. With NO per-tick cap in force there is no ceiling to charge and such a tick really does add 0 — the runner says so, and that is a louder problem than this one; (3) the counter is a LOCAL json file, not the brain, so a second machine running this job gets its own allowance, and deleting the state file (or the 00:00 UTC rollover) restores the whole thing at once; a state file the runner CANNOT WRITE (permissions, a full disk) used to be silently equivalent to one that saved — the total was printed but never landed, so every later tick re-read the stale number and was admitted forever. It now fails closed: pr_review.sh refuses to start a model call and exits 27 with reason=state_unwritable until the path is writable; (4) nothing sums this loop with qa-dream or the dev-loop-* runs — there is no account-level ceiling anywhere, and this number is not one. The cross-job overlap that actually matters is not consumption but the shared rate-limit window and, when the brain's auth mode mints CLI tokens, contention on that credential cache — which is what the shared cross-agent lock (r4_concurrency) exists for. THE ANTHROPIC_API_KEY CASE — the one posture in which this cap really does bound dollars. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, if either is set in the environment, TAKE PRECEDENCE over the subscription credential, and the run then bills as metered API usage. A scheduler job that declares its own environment is safe by construction (it inherits only the variables its definition declares); a hand-run tick inherits the operator's shell, which is exactly where such a variable lives. So pr_review.sh REFUSES a real tick when either is set — exit 28, the first gate of the run, ahead of the lock, the brain gate and any token; presence only is detected, and no key material is ever read, printed or logged. LOOP_PR_REVIEW_ALLOW_API_KEY=1 arms metered billing deliberately: it prints a banner, logs event=metered_api_billing_armed, and FLIPS the framing of every consumption message from that point down — under that override this number is a real spending cap and the runner says so ('THIS ONE IS MONEY'). Every log line carrying a figure also carries spend_basis=list-price-estimate-unbilled or spend_basis=metered-api-billed, so the units are unambiguous on the same line as the number. 60.0 RATIFIES what the runner derives on its own (PER_DAY_USD_FALLBACK_MULTIPLE x the per-tick cap), so adopting the key is a provenance change and not a behaviour change — and it DECOUPLES the day ceiling from a flag that moves, since the derived fallback makes a one-off `--budget-usd 5` silently drop the day to 20. Chosen over a tighter number because the tight direction fails SILENTLY: exit 26 does not call bump_stuck and writes no event=end line, so an exhausted afternoon and a dead loop look identical from outside, and PRs merge while the loop is dark. Chosen over a looser one because loosening a number with zero telemetry is a preference, not a decision. Realistic days are single digits — most of the 24 ticks find an empty queue. read_limits validates only > 0: 0 or a negative FALLS BACK to 4x the per-tick cap rather than stopping anything, so to stop the loop use the R9 pause flag or disarm the scheduler job. Put `grep -E 'reason=daily_budget|reason=state_unwritable|event=spend_assumed' pr-review.log` next to the outcome grep in the daily check. Those field and event names still say `spend` and are deliberately NOT renamed: a silently-renamed field is a runbook grep that stops matching, which is the same class of lie this honesty clause is about — spend_basis= on the same line carries the units instead. Revisit this number against the spend_usd= column after a couple of weeks; the first exit 26 is data to read, not a number to raise reflexively, and the question it answers is 'is this job burning more of the shared window than it is worth', never 'can we afford it'.

ui_parity_sweep.rule: qa-ui-parity-sweep's bounds, from the skill's spec. budget_min is a HARD wall-clock budget for the whole run (capture closes at ~73%, fixes at ~91%, the report is due at 100%); sweep.py init reads it as the --budget-min default and `sweep.py budget` enforces it per phase (exit 3). A late report is written anyway and says BUDGET EXCEEDED. max_fix_prs caps the one-file fixes per run — enforced by `sweep.py fixed` (exit 3 on the third) — and each opens as a DRAFT pull request through infra-ship --draft (the vcs_host adapter's draft option), the one opt-in exception to the no-auto-ship rule for this sweep. max_dialogs_per_route bounds how many dialog triggers the capture opens per route per environment. Raising any of these is a human decision; the sweep never reads them as targets.
